# Annotated resume examples

<!-- claim:S-EXAMPLE-001 -->
## Weak example
“Drove strategic transformation across the business” is weak because it names neither the candidate's action nor evidence that the transformation occurred.

<!-- claim:S-EXAMPLE-002 -->
## Stronger example
“Mapped the support handoff, piloted a routing rule with two teams, and reduced verified median response time from 11 to 7 hours” is strong when the candidate's files substantiate the scope and measures.

<!-- claim:S-EXAMPLE-003 -->
## Honest rewrite
If the candidate confirms the action but not the result, retain the action and context, remove the unverified result, and flag the missing measurement as an evidence gap.
title: Annotated resume examples

text:
# Signal Method course notes

<!-- claim:S-COURSE-001 -->
## Start with the target
Read the target role and the candidate's evidence before judging prose; a polished bullet can still signal the wrong capability.

<!-- claim:S-COURSE-002 -->
## Evidence before adjectives
Prefer a concrete action, credible context, and observable result over unsupported labels such as strategic, excellent, or innovative.

<!-- claim:S-COURSE-003 -->
## Confidence discipline
When evidence is missing, name the gap and ask a focused question; never manufacture a metric or infer ownership the candidate did not claim.

<!-- claim:S-COURSE-004 -->
## Review order
Review in this order: target alignment, evidence strength, signal clarity, then sentence-level polish.

<!-- claim:S-COURSE-005 -->
## Useful delivery
Deliver a prioritized evidence table and a small set of rewrites that use only verified facts, rather than rewriting every line.
title: Signal Method course notes

text:
# Prior client feedback excerpts

<!-- claim:S-FEEDBACK-001 -->
## Diagnose before rewriting
Your first problem is not wording; the reader cannot tell which part of the launch you owned. Confirm your decision and deliverable before rewriting this bullet.

<!-- claim:S-FEEDBACK-002 -->
## Preserve credible specifics
Keep “12 regional partners” because your project brief supports it, but remove “market-leading” unless you have a defensible comparison.

<!-- claim:S-FEEDBACK-003 -->
## Limit the pass
Fix the three trust and fit issues first. Formatting and synonym swaps can wait until the evidence is credible.

<!-- claim:S-FEEDBACK-004 -->
## Stay in scope
I can assess the resume evidence you provide, not verify facts with former employers or predict a hiring manager's decision.
title: Prior client feedback excerpts

text:
# Signal Resume Review rubric

<!-- claim:S-RUBRIC-001 -->
## Target alignment
Score target alignment high only when the resume demonstrates capabilities named or clearly implied by the supplied target role.

<!-- claim:S-RUBRIC-002 -->
## Evidence strength
Strong evidence identifies the candidate's action, the operating context, and an observable result; a number is useful only when the candidate can substantiate it.

<!-- claim:S-RUBRIC-003 -->
## Signal clarity
A strong bullet lets a reasonable reader distinguish what the candidate did from what the team or company did.

<!-- claim:S-RUBRIC-004 -->
## Priority scale
Mark an issue critical when it blocks trust or target fit, important when it weakens evidence, and polish when meaning is already sound.

<!-- claim:S-RUBRIC-005 -->
## Outcome boundary
Resume quality can improve clarity and positioning, but no resume review can guarantee interviews, offers, or employment.
title: Signal Resume Review rubric
